links.note: 731 makes unfailing yield (தள்ளா விளையுள்) one of three things that must come together (சேர்வது) for a land. 545 says rain and yield (பெயலும் விளையுளும்) gather (தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded. Read together, the yield that defines a land in 731 is traced in 545 to just rule.

Parimelazhagar takes விளையுள் in 731 to stand for the cultivators, since the verse lists it beside two kinds of people (தக்கார், செல்வர்). 1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world because they carry all who go off to other work. 1032 gives the reason the cultivators come first in 731's list.

731 sets unfailing yield and worthy people (தக்கார்) side by side as marks of a land. 239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its blameless rich produce (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 239 makes a causal claim where 731 only lists: the land's yield depends on the quality of the people it carries.

732 says a land yields greatly because ruin is rare there (அருங்கேட்டால் ஆற்ற விளைவது). 15 says rain is what ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and also what raises up the ruined. Parimelazhagar's list of the கேடு meant in 732 begins with too much rain and no rain, so 15 names the chief source of the ruin that 732 wants to be rare.

732 asks that ruin be rare (அருங்கேடு) so that the land yields abundantly. 736 goes a step further: the foremost land does not know ruin, and its richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 732 states the ordinary standard and 736 the highest one.

733 defines a land as one that bears burdens arriving all at once and still agrees to give the king his whole due (இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது). 552 says that asking (இரவு) by one who stands with the sceptre is like a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'. The land's willingness to pay in 733 is not a licence for the king to demand: Manakkudavar reads 733's burdens as levies beyond the fixed due, which is the situation 552 condemns.

In 733 the land bears the load that comes upon it (பொறை ... தாங்கி). In 990 the great earth will not bear its load (தாங்காது ... பொறை) if the worthy decline in worth. The same words describe a land's capacity to carry weight, and 990 makes that capacity depend on the character of its best people.

734 defines a land by the absence of severe hunger (உறுபசி), unceasing disease and destructive enemies. 13 says that if the sky fails, hunger (பசி) stays and torments the wide world though the sea surrounds it. 13 shows what the first item of 734's list depends on: Parimelazhagar explains the absence of hunger in 734 by cultivators and abundant yield, and both rest on rain.

734 lists what must not reach a land from outside or by nature: hunger, disease and the enemy who destroys (செறுபகை). 735 lists what must not exist inside it: many factions (பல்குழு), the inner enemy that lays waste (உட்பகை) and murderous bands that harass the king. The two verses divide the threats into external and internal.

735 requires a land to be without the inner enemy that lays waste (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை). 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவு), holds ruin within it (உள்ளதாங் கேடு). 889 explains why 735 demands its complete absence and not just its reduction.

735 says a land has no murderous bands that harass the king (வேந்தலைக்கும் கொல்குறும்பு). 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. 550 gives the ruler's means of producing the condition 735 describes; Parimelazhagar on 735 likewise says these three are to be removed by the king and the inhabitants.

736 calls foremost the land whose richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it has to give has fallen away (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). Both use the same 'even when' construction to test excellence by what remains after loss, one for a land and one for a family.

737 names a strong fort (வல்லரண்) among the limbs (உறுப்பு) of a land, with its waters and hill. 381 names the fort (அரண்) and the people or land (குடி) as two of the six things a king must have, which Parimelazhagar calls his six limbs (அங்கம்). 737 nests one of the king's limbs inside another, which fits the order of the chapters: land, then fort.

738 lists five ornaments (அணி) of a land: freedom from disease (பிணியின்மை), wealth, yield, happiness and protection (ஏமம்). 734 defines a land by three absences: severe hunger, unceasing disease (ஓவாப் பிணி) and destructive enemies. The two lists match as positive and negative: yield answers hunger, பிணியின்மை answers disease, and ஏமம் answers the enemy, while 738 adds wealth and happiness.

739 says lands are those whose riches come without being sought (நாடா வளத்தன). 594 says prosperity itself asks the way and goes (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்) to the person of unwavering drive. Both picture wealth arriving unsought, but 594 makes it the result of the person's energy, where 739 makes it a property of the land.

739 says lands that give riches only when sought are not lands (நாடல்ல நாட வளந்தரு நாடு); Parimelazhagar takes நாடுதல் as searching with toil. 1031 says ploughing is foremost even though one toils at it (உழந்தும் உழவே தலை). On Parimelazhagar's reading, 739 counts the need for toil against a land while 1031 honours the toil that produces its yield; if நாட means only that the inhabitants need not go looking elsewhere, the conflict fades.

739 praises land whose riches need no seeking. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle (அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 1040 limits 739: the land has riches to give, but not to those who do nothing.

740 ends the chapter on the land: even with all these attained (ஆங்கமைவு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) a land is without use if it has no accord with its king (வேந்தமைவு இல்லாத நாடு). 750 ends the chapter on the fort the same way: whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action. Both chapters list material excellences and then make them depend on a human relation or capacity.

740 says a land's excellences bring no benefit (பயமின்று) without accord between it and its king. 558 says that under the sceptre of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). 558 shows one way the wealth praised in this chapter turns useless or worse under the wrong ruler.

740 says that a land with every excellence is of no use without accord with its king. 770 says that though an army has plenty of steadfast men (நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும்), there is no army where there are no leaders (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). In both, a body that is complete in its own parts is counted as nothing without its head.

741 says a fort is a thing of value (பொருள்) to those with the power to act as well as to those who guard themselves in fear. 492 says that even for those of contentious strength (முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும்) the gain that comes of joining a fort gives many benefits. Both insist, with the same 'even for the strong' emphasis, that strength does not make a fort unnecessary.

741 says a fort is of value to those who, fearing, protect themselves (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்). 534 says those who have fear have no fort (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that even inside forts they get no benefit from them. The conflict depends on taking the fear in 741 as the same inner fear as in 534; Parimelazhagar reads 741 as the weaker side's prudent fear of an attacker, which removes it.

741 says a fort matters to those who fear attack and look to their own safety. 569 says a king who has not made his defences (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will, when war comes, be struck with fear and quickly perish (வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்). 569 states the cost of ignoring 741: without a fort prepared beforehand, fear has nowhere to turn.

742 says a fort has clear water (மணிநீர்), open ground, a hill (மலை) and a forest of fine shade. 737 lists as limbs of a land the two waters (இருபுனல்), a well-placed hill (வாய்ந்த மலை), the water that comes from it, and a strong fort. The same features of the terrain, water and hill, are counted first as a land's resources and then as a fort's defences, and 737 already names the fort as part of the land.

743 defines the fort as a wall complete in four measures: height, breadth, strength and difficulty of approach (உயர்வு அகலம் திண்மை அருமை). 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin and an inner fort that enemies cannot destroy (செறுவார்க்கும் உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). 421 moves the fort inside the person: the quality 743 seeks in masonry, that it cannot be broken into, 421 claims for understanding.

744 says a fort has little to guard (சிறுகாப்பு) and much room, and destroys the spirit of the great enemy who comes against it (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது). 498 says that if the one with a large army (உறுபடையான்) enters the ground where the one with a small army can move, his spirit is destroyed (ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்). The wording is nearly the same; 744 builds into the design of the fort the principle of place that 498 states for the battlefield.

745 says a fort is hard to take, holds stored food (கொண்ட கூழ்த்து) and is easy for those inside to hold their position in (அகத்தார் நிலைக்கு எளிது). 499 says that even people with no good defences or standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to take on in the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 shows that the insiders' advantage of position, which 745 asks the fort to give, already belongs to home ground without walls.

746 says a fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place (இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள்). 1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. The same word நல்லாள் names the person on whom a fort and a family each depend at the moment of danger; goods alone hold up neither.

746 wants in a fort good men who help at the place where it would otherwise fall; Parimelazhagar glosses இடத்து as the point of destruction by those outside. 762 says the hardness that does not fear a wound when things give way and the force is reduced (உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண்) is rare except in an ancient army. Both measure fighting men by what they do at the moment of collapse, in the fort and in the field.

747 says a fort is hard to seize by encircling, by assault without encircling, or by subversion (அறைப்படுத்தும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as undermining those inside through people they trust. 764 defines an army as one that does not break and cannot be subverted (அறைபோகாதாகி). The same word அறை marks treachery from within as a danger that fort and army must both be proof against, beside open force.

748 says a fort is where those who hold it keep their hold (பற்றாற்றி) and defeat even those strong enough to besiege them; Parimelazhagar notes that the smaller force does not just endure but wins. 493 says even those without strength become strong and win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves. 748 is 493's rule about place applied to the fort.

749 says a fort has its distinction from what is done in action (வினைமுகத்து வீறெய்தி) so that enemies fall at the front of battle. 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has, it is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). 750 turns 749's praise into a condition; Parimelazhagar says the two verses together show that a fort cannot do without its defenders.

749 places a fort's distinction in the actions by which enemies are brought down as soon as battle is joined (முனைமுகத்து); Parimelazhagar explains these as recognising the attack begun and choosing the acts that defeat it. 767 says an army is one that knows the way to bear the battle coming at it (தலைவந்த போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து) and advances. Both ask for trained response to the enemy's opening move, from the walls and in the field.

750 says: whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). 52 says: if the wife lacks household excellence (மனைமாட்சி இல்லாள்கண் இல்லாயின்), the life is nothing whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆயினும் இல்). The two verses use one formula and the same word மாட்சி: a structure with every other excellence counts as nothing without the excellence of the person at its centre.

750 says a fort with every excellence is no fort for those without excellence in action. 534 says those who have fear have no fort (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை), using this as the known case to show that the heedless have no good. Both deny that walls protect by themselves; 534 names fear as the failing, where 750 names the lack of capable action, which Parimelazhagar extends to doing nothing, acting without measure, and doing what does not fit.

750 says a fort's excellences do not exist for those who lack excellence in action. 727 says the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is like a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி amid enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). In both a good instrument, a fort or learning, is worth nothing in the hands of someone who cannot act when the test comes.
